name: Gemmotherapy

card.summary: Gemmotherapy uses extracts of plant buds and young shoots, marketed for their antioxidant polyphenol content, including in skin and age-related wellness contexts.
card.note: Wikipedia describes it as pseudoscientific and notes no randomized double-blind studies; products are bud macerates in glycerin, water and alcohol.

quick.overview:
Gemmotherapy is a branch of herbal medicine built on extracts of buds, young shoots and other embryonic plant tissue. Proponents say these tissues are rich in polyphenols, vitamins and growth-related compounds, and some brands position them as antioxidant support for skin and ageing.

Research is mostly chemical analysis and laboratory or animal work. A 2026 review calls it a branch of phytotherapy with a distinctive phytochemical profile, while Wikipedia describes it as pseudoscientific and notes no randomized double-blind studies.
quick.how: Bud extracts are sold as liquid concentrated macerates, typically made in a glycerin, water and ethanol mix, and are taken by the drop in water or used in some cosmetics.
quick.risks: Little safety data exists from human trials. Preparations contain ethanol. Anyone with a medical condition or on medication is generally advised to consult a clinician.

lead: Gemmotherapy is a form of phytotherapy using extracts from plant meristematic tissue such as buds, young shoots and sprouts [1]. Pol Henry, a Belgian homeopath, developed it in the late 1950s as "phytoembryotherapy," and it entered the French Pharmacopoeia in 1965 [2].

Proponents say the embryonic, metabolically active tissues are a concentrated source of polyphenols, phytohormones, amino acids, vitamins and enzymes, with synergistic activity [1]. Reviews describe bud extracts as antioxidant adjuvants in metabolic and age-related conditions [3], which is the chain by which they are linked to skin and ageing.

Wikipedia describes gemmotherapy as pseudoscientific and states that it has not been the subject of randomized double-blind studies [2]. Published work includes chemical profiling of bud macerates [4], and laboratory or animal studies on antioxidant, antimicrobial and organ-protective effects [5][6][7].

chain: Bud extracts supply polyphenols and antioxidants
Claimed support for skin and healthy ageing
angle.text: Gemmotherapy extracts are marketed as antioxidant-rich botanicals for general wellness and ageing. Any skin benefit is a claim by proponents; the cited research is mostly chemical and laboratory work.

infobox: Black currant, rose hip, rosemary, linden, alder

paras: Concentrated bud macerates are made from buds and young shoots by maceration in a solvent of glycerin, water and ethanol in equal parts [4]. Studied examples include Alnus glutinosa, Ribes nigrum, Rosa canina, Rosmarinus officinalis and Tilia tomentosa [4].
Pol Henry began investigating the approach in the late 1950s with French homeopaths, first calling it phytoembryotherapy; it was included in the Pharmacopée Française in 1965 [2].

Content varies with harvest time and location: a study of Czech tree buds found variable phenolic content and antioxidant potential [8]. Laboratory studies report antimicrobial effects of extracts such as dog rose, sea buckthorn and hawthorn [9]. A black currant bud extract was examined in a pilot study for neuroprotective effects and effects on TNF-alpha [10], and a hazelnut bud extract in a mouse model of liver fibrosis [5]. A 2024 Cureus report described use of Sorbus domestica in Meniere's disease [6].

No controlled human trials on skin or appearance outcomes were identified. A 2024 Cureus report looked at Sorbus domestica in Meniere's disease [6]; the rest of the literature consists of chemical analysis, laboratory and animal work [4][5][8][9][10].
